title: MosquitoCoilClear
question: How does a mosquito coil work?
hook: A mosquito coil is a slow fuse wound into a spiral: nearly 70 cm of pressed powder that an ember crosses at 1.4 mm a minute, warming a few milligrams of insecticide into the air just ahead of itself. See why it is a spiral, what the vapour does to a mosquito's nerves, and why opening a window cuts the smoke and the protection by exactly the same share.

explainer.title: Two spirals, a stand and an ember
explainer.text: A coil comes as a flat disc that is really two spirals nested together; you snap them apart and stand one on a metal prong. It is a slow-burning base of sawdust, coconut-shell powder or charcoal powder, a binder, dye and fragrance, and the part that matters: a synthetic pyrethroid insecticide. Indian labels show 0.005% to 0.1% for the common coils, so a 13 gram coil carries only a few milligrams.

explainer.title: A night-long fuse in a 12 cm disc
explainer.text: The length of a spiral is very nearly the area of its ring divided by the spacing of its turns: about 68 cm for a common coil. The ember creeps at about 1.4 mm a minute, so the coil lasts about eight hours. The glow itself would destroy the insecticide, but heat runs a few millimetres ahead of it, and at 150 to 300 °C the active turns to vapour and leaves before the fire arrives.

explainer.title: Gates held open
explainer.text: A mosquito finds you by the carbon dioxide in your breath from 10 to 50 metres, by your shape from 5 to 15 metres and by your warmth in the last metre. Her nerves fire using sodium channels that open for a thousandth of a second. A pyrethroid holds them open, so one touch becomes a burst of signals: at a faint dose she is restless and fails to bite, at a higher dose she is knocked down. Insect channels grip pyrethroids about a thousand times more strongly than mammal ones, and a warm body and a liver do the rest. Cats and fish are sensitive.

explainer.title: The window cuts both
explainer.text: A coil adds two things to a room: the vapour, and smoke. Chamber tests found 63 to 127 mg of fine particles (PM2.5) an hour from ordinary coils, enough to lift a shut 30 m³ bedroom into the thousands of micrograms per cubic metre, against a WHO guideline of 15 for a day's average. One coil gives off as much PM2.5 mass as 75 to 137 cigarettes, which measures the dust released, not what a sleeper breathes. Fresh air removes the same share of smoke and vapour: there is no setting that clears one and keeps the other.

explainer.title: The same idea without the ember, and without the chemical
explainer.text: Liquid vaporisers and mats warm a similar active with a small electric heater, so there is no smoke from burning. Nets, screens, fans and emptying standing water add nothing to the air at all, and a treated bed net is the WHO's main recommendation where malaria spreads. Coils do cut bites, but a Cochrane review found we do not know whether they prevent malaria. Ultrasonic gadgets have failed every fair field test.

explainer.title: Rules, care and resistance
explainer.text: In India a coil is an insecticide product under the Insecticides Act, 1968: it must be registered, and the pack must show the active, its strength and a registration number. Use it on its stand, away from bedding, with some fresh air. Where pyrethroids are used heavily, mosquitoes carrying a slightly different sodium channel survive and multiply; this knock-down resistance has been found in India's malaria and dengue mosquitoes. India reported about 2.6 lakh malaria cases and 2.3 lakh dengue cases in 2024.

concepts.def: A spiral of pressed, slow-burning powder that carries a little insecticide and smoulders for hours.
A synthetic insecticide modelled on pyrethrins, the natural insect-killers of pyrethrum daisies.
A spiral with evenly spaced turns; its length is about the area of its ring divided by the spacing.
Burning without a flame: a glowing ember creeping through a solid.
A protein gate in a nerve's membrane that opens briefly to make a voltage spike. Pyrethroids hold it open.
Mosquitoes avoiding or leaving a space because of a chemical in its air.
The mass of particles finer than 2.5 micrometres in a cubic metre of air.
How many room-fulls of fresh air replace the old air each hour.
A small change in an insect's sodium channel that makes pyrethroids bind less well, spread by selection.
